extracted.intended_audience: research funders, grant program managers, and policy-makers interested in alternative allocation mechanisms
extracted.subtask_description: Design and implementation guidance for a two-stage 'modified lottery' grant-allocation process: conventional peer review used as a threshold filter to identify meritorious applications, followed by random allocation among those meritorious applications up to the budget. Includes implementation variants (tie-breaker, targeted schemes) and empirical considerations about acceptance and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 1 — Conventional peer review as a sufficiency filter
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications scored on standard criteria; each application classified as meritorious or non-meritorious; non-meritorious applications can be revised and resubmitted; no fine-grained ranking required at this stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage 1 is intended to determine whether an application meets a quality threshold (sufficiency) rather than to produce a fine-grained ranked list. Reviewers should apply existing criteria but focus on binary determination of meritoriousness. Avoid requiring fine-grained ranking or precise ordinal comparisons among applications in this stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 2 — Random allocation among meritorious applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer randomly generates priority scores for all meritorious applications and funding is awarded based on randomly generated scores up to the budget limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage 2 replaces fine-grained ranking with an explicit randomization procedure (lottery) among those applications passing the Stage 1 threshold. Implementations may generate random priority scores or otherwise randomly select winners until funds are exhausted. Ensure transparency and auditable randomization procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening criteria for meritorious classification (example: HRC Explorer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications screened for feasibility, ethics, and innovativeness (example from Health Research Council of New Zealand’s Explorer Grant scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a small set of clear, defensible screening criteria that determine meritorious status (e.g., feasibility, ethical acceptability, potential innovativeness or impact). Keep criteria focused and simple to support rapid binary decisions by reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as tie-breaker for borderline applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Lottery used as a tie-breaker for applications that are judged borderline or indistinguishable by reviewers (implemented by Swiss NSF and Volkswagen Foundation as tie-breakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply randomization only to the subset of applications where reviewers indicate uncertainty or where scores are effectively indistinguishable. This variant preserves more conventional ranking when clear differences exist but uses lottery to resolve ties and reduce burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted/transformative-scheme implementation (example: HRC Explorer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the modified-lottery to specific funding lines targeting exploratory or transformative research ideas with major potential impact (Explorer Grant model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lotteries where goals include high-risk/high-reward or transformative research, where conventional peer review may be especially conservative. Tailor screening criteria to the program’s mission (e.g., innovativeness, potential impact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate fine-grained reviewer-judgment noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Design criterion: eliminates fine-grained reviewer-judgment noise — evidence shows fine-grained judgments are essentially random in the fundable range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given empirical evidence of low reliability among near-fundable applications, avoid designing systems that rely on precise ordinal distinctions among otherwise meritorious proposals. Prefer thresholding plus random selection to reduce spurious precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce bias in allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design criterion: reduces bias — disparities at the scoring stage (e.g., gender, institution) are reduced by removing fine-grained scoring from final decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bias often operates in fine-grained score differences and panel dynamics, using a lottery after meritorious screening can blunt systematic disparities. Track outcome demographics to monitor impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce conservatism against novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Design criterion: reduces conservatism — avoids penalties against novelty that arise in conventional review (novel proposals less likely to receive high fine-grained scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By preventing marginal ranking penalties for novelty, lotteries can increase the funding share of riskier, potentially more innovative projects. Consider program targeting (e.g., exploratory grants) to amplify this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce applicant preparation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Design criterion: reduces application-preparation costs — applicants only need to demonstrate meritoriousness rather than optimize applications for granular ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpler threshold criteria and acceptance of randomness in final selection can shorten applications and reduce time spent tailoring proposals for marginal score improvements. Communicate expectations to applicants about scope/length and evaluation focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce reviewer burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Design criterion: reduces reviewer burden — binary classification (meritorious/non-meritorious) is faster and less onerous than nuanced ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure reviewer tasks to make pass/fail judgments on a small set of criteria. This can increase throughput and reviewer willingness to participate; consider streamlined review forms and shorter reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve diversity of awardees
rubrics_metrics.description: Design criterion: improves diversity — empirical implementations observed increased representation (e.g., lottery before/after review increased female PI share in some studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor demographic outcomes and consider lottery variants that have evidence of improving representation. Use targeted schemes or randomized selection timing (e.g., before/after review) to maximize desired diversity effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspects explicitly removed by modified-lottery among meritorious applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The modified-lottery explicitly removes the following from grant decisions among meritorious applications: fine-grained scoring of significance; comparative ranking on innovation; subjective judgment of investigator promise; panel deliberation effects; reviewer expertise matching; score-aggregation procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry lists practices the modified-lottery seeks to eliminate from marginal selection decisions. If adopting a lottery, be explicit about which traditional evaluative practices will no longer determine funding among meritorious applications, and explain rationale to stakeholders to maintain legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for hybrid models to increase community acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding/design recommendation: most scientists oppose pure lotteries but support hybrid models; acceptance is higher among those who have won lottery funding, underrepresented researchers, and those with shorter track records; lower among senior researchers and fields with high consensus norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should consider hybrid approaches (thresholding plus lottery or lottery-as-tie-breaker) and include communication strategies, pilot studies, and stakeholder engagement to increase legitimacy. Track and report survey/acceptance data to inform broader adoption.
